filesystem-service.name: filesystem service
filesystem-service.short: The one protocol-neutral interface every adapter calls. It decides and orders each file operation.
filesystem-service.long: The one protocol-neutral interface (`vfs.Service`) every adapter calls; it orders each client operation and routes it to the primary that serves it. Defined by RFC 17.
filesystem-service.clash: Not an [[auxiliary-service]], which is protocol code beside an adapter, nor a Windows RPC service such as srvsvc. The package is named `vfs`, but it is not the Linux kernel's VFS.

share.name: share
share.short: A file tree the server offers to clients; NFS calls it an export. Each share has its own settings, snapshots and journal limits.
share.long: A file tree the server exports to clients, with its own settings, snapshots and journal limits. NFS calls it an export; NFS and SMB clients both reach the same shares.

node.name: node
node.short: One DittoFS server process. Every node runs every component.
node.long: One DittoFS server process, built by `node.New`; every node runs every component and can be a primary or a replica.

primary.name: primary
primary.short: The one node that orders and accepts the writes to a set of files, its [[shard]]. On a single node, that node is the primary of every share.
primary.long: The one node that orders and accepts a shard's writes, as its shard record names. On a single node, that node is the primary of every share.

gateway-node.name: gateway node
gateway-node.short: (cluster) The node a client's call arrives at. It forwards the call to the primary and decides nothing itself.
gateway-node.long: (cluster) The node a client's call arrives at. Its `vfs.Gateway` forwards the call to the primary when it is not the primary itself, and decides nothing.

open-state.name: open state
open-state.short: The record of who holds a file open, locked or cached. It covers opens, deny modes, byte-range locks and caching grants.
open-state.long: Who holds a file open, locked or cached; the only thing besides a name that keeps a file alive. Decided at the file's primary (RFC 14).

deny-mode.name: deny mode
deny-mode.short: The access an open refuses to every other open for as long as it is held. It is checked when an open is granted and on every [[anonymous-open|read or write made without an open]], such as an NFSv3 write.
deny-mode.long: The access an open refuses to every other open while it is held — SMB's deny-write, for example. Checked both ways when an open is granted, and on every [[anonymous-open|anonymous]] read or write.
deny-mode.clash: SMB spells it backwards: `ShareAccess` lists what other opens may do, and the deny mode is its complement over read, write and delete.

handle.name: handle
handle.short: What a client holds to name a file. It contains the share and the file's ID, never a path, and stays valid across restarts.
handle.long: What a client holds to name a file. It contains the share and the file's ID, never a path, and stays valid across server restarts.
handle.clash: An NFS file handle names a file. An SMB **durable handle** is an open kept across a disconnect, and an SMB `FileId` names an open, not a file. The [[journal]]'s `Handle` is something else again: one share's access to the journal, not a file handle.

caching-grant.name: caching grant
caching-grant.short: The server's promise to a client that nobody else is using a file, so the client may cache it. NFS calls it a delegation, SMB an oplock or a lease, and the server takes it back with a recall.
caching-grant.long: The server's promise that nobody else is using a file — an NFS delegation, an SMB oplock or SMB lease — taken back by a [[recall]] within a bounded time.

retry-later.name: retry-later (ErrDelay)
retry-later.short: The protocol-neutral error for a call that will succeed if tried again shortly. It carries the reason for the delay.
retry-later.long: The neutral error for a call that will succeed shortly, carrying its cause. NFS answers `NFS4ERR_DELAY` / `NFS3ERR_JUKEBOX`; SMB [[held-request|holds the request]] pending as long as its cause allows, and answers a cause never held at once.

anonymous-open.name: anonymous open
anonymous-open.short: What an NFSv3 read or write, or NFSv4 I/O under the anonymous stateid, runs against instead of an open. It carries only the caller's identity and no state.
anonymous-open.long: What an NFSv3 read or write, or NFSv4 I/O under the anonymous stateid, runs against instead of an [[open]]: the caller's identity, and no state.

admission.name: admission
admission.short: The checks every call passes at its [[share]] before the file's own permissions: whether the share is serving, whether the caller signed in strongly enough and from an allowed address, which user it acts as there, and whether the share can take another request.
admission.long: The per-share checks every call passes before the permission check: the share's state, its flavours, its client rules, squashing, then the share's cap on request buffers. The [[filesystem-service|service]]'s, never an adapter's.
admission.clash: Not the adapter pipeline's admit stage, which only charges the connection's flow control (an SMB credit, an NFSv4.1 slot or a cap of 64 requests) before the request is decoded. Nor the [[admission-lock|admission lock]] or [[fold-admission|fold admission]].

adapter.name: adapter
adapter.short: The code for one wire protocol, from the listening socket to the call into the filesystem service. It decides nothing about files.
adapter.long: The code for one wire protocol: framing, compounds, replay caches, error codes, and nothing else. It turns bytes into service calls and answers into bytes.
adapter.clash: The [[remote-block-store|remote block store]] layer also calls each backend (S3, memory) an adapter, and [[adapter-bytes|Adapter bytes]] are opaque data a protocol adapter stores in [[open-state|open state]]. On its own, adapter always means a protocol adapter.

core.name: core
core.short: The adapter package shared by every protocol. It holds what is the same everywhere, written once: listeners, connections, the pipeline and drain.
core.long: `internal/adapter/core`: what is the same for every protocol, written once — listeners, connections, the pipeline, the compound runner, [[held-request|held requests]], middleware, the error-table type. Pooled buffers are not core's: they belong to `pkg/resources` (RFC 24).

pipeline.name: pipeline
pipeline.short: The fixed sequence of stages every request goes through. A request is framed, decoded, admitted, checked for replay and resolved, then the service is called and its answer is mapped, encoded and sent.
pipeline.long: The fixed sequence of stages every request passes, one implementation for every protocol. Each step is a **stage**; a protocol plugs in its own framer, header codec, flow control, replay check and error table.

codec.name: codec
codec.short: Pure functions that turn bytes into a request's fields, and a reply's fields back into bytes. A codec does no I/O and never calls the service.
codec.long: Pure functions that turn bytes into a request's fields and a reply's fields into bytes: no I/O, no service, no clock, no setting. That purity is what makes golden vectors and fuzzing possible.
codec.clash: The [[metadata-store|metadata store]] uses the word for how one stored value is encoded, a [[value-codec|store codec]]: the same idea of pure encoding, at a different layer.

handler.name: handler
handler.short: The function for one wire operation. It takes the request's fields, makes at most one service call that changes anything, and returns the reply's fields.
handler.long: The function for one wire operation: fields in, at most one service call that changes state, fields out. It decides nothing on a file's attributes, mode or ACL.

operation-table.name: operation table
operation-table.short: A table with one row per wire operation. Each row names the operation's handler and the preconditions the pipeline checks before running it.
operation-table.long: One row per wire operation: its codec and handler, plus the columns the pipeline checks first — what it needs, which versions serve it, whether it is cacheable, its largest reply.

error-table.name: error table
error-table.short: A table, one per protocol, that maps every protocol-neutral service error to a status on the wire. A test proves that no error is left out.
error-table.long: One per protocol: maps each neutral service error to the protocol's status. Every error must have a row; one without is answered server fault and logged at error.

connection-state.name: connection state
connection-state.short: What a protocol keeps for each connection or session, such as slots, credits, reply caches, keys and ID tables. It lives in memory only.
connection-state.long: What the protocol keeps per connection or session: slot tables, reply caches, credits, security contexts, ID tables. The adapter owns it, in memory only, and never writes or replicates it.

client-held-name.name: client-held name
client-held-name.short: Anything a client can present again after its connection is gone, such as a file handle, a stateid or a durable handle.
client-held-name.long: Anything a client can present again after its connection is gone — a file handle, a stateid, a durable handle, a create verifier. What it names must outlive the connection, so it is never the adapter's.

compound.name: compound
compound.short: Several operations sent in one request, as NFSv4 COMPOUND and SMB compounded requests do. The adapter runs them one after another, each with its own handler.
compound.long: Several operations in one request — NFSv4 `COMPOUND`, SMB compounded requests. The adapter's compound runner runs them as a sequence of handlers, each a separate service call, with no lock held across them.

held-request.name: held request
held-request.short: An SMB request that has to wait. The server answers STATUS_PENDING and the pipeline runs the call again later, because SMB has no way to tell a client to retry.
held-request.long: An SMB request whose answer is to wait: it gets the interim `STATUS_PENDING` and the pipeline re-drives the call later. Between attempts it is a timer and the decoded request, not a worker.

callback.name: callback
callback.short: A call in the other direction: the service needs a client to do something the client did not ask for, such as give back a lease, and the adapter delivers the request.
callback.long: The service calling a client: a lease break, a change notification, a granted lock, a revocation. The adapter registers a `Callbacks` value at `Connect` and delivers each one: on the client's own connection, or for NLM by connecting out to the host.

auxiliary-service.name: auxiliary service
auxiliary-service.short: A protocol beside an adapter's main one that calls the filesystem service or holds client state, such as NFS's MOUNT, NLM and NSM.
auxiliary-service.long: A service beside an adapter's main protocol that reaches the filesystem service or holds client state the protocol depends on — today NFS's MOUNT, NLM and NSM. Part of its adapter: same pipeline, starts and stops with it.

sidecar.name: sidecar
sidecar.short: Something run beside the adapters that calls no service and holds no client state, such as mDNS or the port mapper.
sidecar.long: Something the node runs beside one or more adapters that reaches no service and holds no client state — mDNS, WS-Discovery, the port mapper, rpcbind registration. Its failure fails only itself.

recording-service.name: recording wrapper
recording-service.short: A test wrapper around the [[in-memory-service|in-memory service]] that records each call and passes it through, never answering in its place. Handler tests read its record to check that a request made one mutating call.
recording-service.long: Lives in `vfstest`, around the real `*vfs.Filesystem` of the in-memory service. It keeps each call with its reference and its answer and passes it through, so a test asserts on what reached the service: a handler test fails when a request leaves more than one mutating call. Error answers come from a separate fault wrapper.

null-service.name: null service
null-service.short: A filesystem service that answers every call at once from memory. Only the allocation gate and the benchmarks use it, to measure the adapter's own cost; nothing checks its answers.
null-service.long: A `vfs.Service` that answers every call at once, so the pipeline benchmarks and the allocation gate measure the adapter's own cost per request, with no storage underneath. It is a load, not a test double: nothing asserts on its answers. The `core` layer's tests run on the [[in-memory-service|in-memory service]] instead.

reference-server.name: reference server
reference-server.short: A widely deployed implementation of a protocol whose wire behaviour DittoFS is compared against.
reference-server.long: A widely deployed implementation of the protocol (Appendix C of RFC 20 names them) whose wire behaviour DittoFS is compared against, field by field.

wire-test.name: wire test
wire-test.short: One scripted request sequence sent to a reference server and to DittoFS, captured and compared field by field.
wire-test.long: A script of requests run against a reference server and against DittoFS; both captures are dissected, normalised and compared field by field. A difference is a bug or a recorded divergence citing an RFC rule.

drain.name: drain
drain.short: Stopping gently. The server accepts no new connections, lets the requests in flight finish, then closes every connection.
drain.long: While a node drains, it accepts no new connection but keeps reading the open ones. Requests that release or flush state run, and so do those already handed to the service. Any other new request gets a move signal only when the service names another node for its share; otherwise it gets no reply (over SMB, an interim `STATUS_PENDING` that returns its credits), and the client sends it again after it reconnects. Draining ends when no request is left, or at the drain deadline.

identity.name: Identity
identity.short: What the security handshake proved about a caller, in protocol-neutral terms: how strong the proof was, how messages are protected, the IDs the caller claims, its address and the evidence.
identity.long: What the handshake proved, and nothing more. `Proof` says how strongly the caller was authenticated (None < Claimed < Secret < Ticket) and `Protection` how messages are protected (None < Integrity < Privacy); it also carries the claimed IDs, the client's address and the `Evidence`. It is built afresh for each request.

flow-control.name: flow control
flow-control.short: The limit on how many requests a client may have in flight. It uses NFSv4.1 slots and SMB credits, and a fixed cap of 64 per connection.
flow-control.long: The bound on requests in flight per connection: the protocol's own where it has one (NFSv4.1 slots, SMB [[credit|credits]]), and a fixed cap of 64 per connection where it has none and on every NFS connection. A connection at its bound is simply not read.

session.name: session
session.short: A protocol's per-client context inside the adapter, either an SMB session or an NFSv4.1 session. It is lost on restart, by design.
session.long: A protocol's per-client context held by the adapter, in memory: an SMB session (keys, signing, trees) or an NFSv4.1 session (slots, reply cache). After a node loss the client rebuilds it.
session.clash: An SMB session (sign-in, keys, trees) and an NFSv4.1 session (slots and reply cache) are different things that share a name; both are connection state.

rpc.name: RPC
rpc.short: The name of two unrelated protocols. ONC RPC carries NFS and its auxiliary services; DCE/RPC runs over SMB's IPC$.
rpc.long: ONC RPC frames NFS, MOUNT, NLM and NSM. DCE/RPC (MS-RPCE) carries Windows share enumeration and name lookups over SMB named pipes on `IPC$`.
rpc.clash: ONC RPC (NFS) and DCE/RPC (SMB's `IPC$`) share only a name. DCE/RPC stays under the SMB adapter, and its `dcerpc` package imports no SMB code.

lease.name: lease
lease.short: A word for three different things. An SMB lease lets a client cache a file. A [[client-lease|client lease]] is how long the server keeps a silent client's state, and a [[node-lease|node lease]] is what a node renews to keep serving.
lease.long: An SMB lease is a caching grant. A [[client-lease|client lease]] is how long the server keeps a silent client's state. A [[node-lease|node lease]] (cluster) is the lease a node renews to keep serving.
lease.clash: SMB lease ≠ client lease ≠ node lease. An SMB lease break is a caching grant being recalled.

engine.name: engine
engine.short: The part of a node that handles file content. It drives the [[journal]], where writes land first, and the components that upload them to the [[remote-tier|remote tier]] and fetch them back, and it decides when each of those happens.
engine.long: The content path of a node (RFC 8): it drives the [[journal]], [[carver]], [[syncer]] and block metadata and decides their policy, one per node with a [[storage-binding|storage binding]] per share. The journal's caller in normal running: it decides what to [[offload]], [[evict]] and [[repack]].

extent.name: extent
extent.short: A contiguous region of one file's bytes, given by an offset and a length. It describes a range; it is not something stored.
extent.long: A contiguous `(offset, length)` region of one file's bytes, and the only term for it. It says which bytes of the file — never where on disk they sit, nor what content they hold.

chunk.name: chunk
chunk.short: A run of one file's bytes, about 256 KiB, cut at a content-defined boundary and named by a keyed hash of its content.
chunk.long: A run of one file's bytes, about 256 KiB, cut at a content-defined boundary and named by its chunk ID, a keyed hash of its content. The journal knows nothing about chunks: a [[record]] is not a chunk.

block.name: block
block.short: The object the remote tier stores. It holds a whole number of chunks written by one upload, 4 MiB by default.
block.long: The object the [[remote-tier]] stores: a whole number of [[chunk|chunks]], written by one put. It targets a configured size, 4 MiB by default and settable from 1 MiB to 64 MiB; a chunk never spans two blocks.

remote-tier.name: remote tier
remote-tier.short: The object storage behind the journals, where offloaded content is held — an S3 bucket, for example.
remote-tier.long: The object storage behind the journals, where [[offload|offloaded]] content is held — an S3 bucket, for example (RFC 4). The journal never speaks to it; the [[engine]] does.

carver.name: carver
carver.short: The component that cuts a file's bytes waiting for upload into [[chunk|chunks]], names each one by a hash of its content and packs the chunks into [[block|blocks]].
carver.long: The component (RFC 2) that cuts a stretch of bytes into content-defined [[chunk|chunks]], hashes each, and packs them into blocks. It runs over the extents the journal [[offer|offers]].

syncer.name: syncer
syncer.short: The component that moves [[block|blocks]] to and from the [[remote-tier|remote tier]]. Its uploader puts whole blocks, and its fetcher gets them back.
syncer.long: The component (RFC 3) that moves [[block|blocks]] to and from the [[remote-tier]]: its uploader puts whole blocks, its fetcher gets chunks or blocks back. Despite the name, it is not what [[sync|syncs]] the journal.

dirty.name: Dirty
dirty.short: Said of bytes only the journal holds, because no current chunk covers them yet. They are served locally and are never evicted.
dirty.long: Said of bytes the journal holds that no current chunk covers yet, so the journal is their only copy. They are served locally and never evicted. In the journal, a dirty extent is a [[held-extent|held extent]] whose [[offloaded-bit]] is unset. Every write starts dirty.

durable.name: durable
durable.short: Kept where a crash cannot lose it. For the journal, that means on its local device after a sync.
durable.long: Held where a crash cannot lose it: by a journal's device after a [[sync]], or by every replica's journal (cluster). Not the remote-tier sense.
durable.clash: Not an SMB **durable handle** or [[smb-durable-open|durable open]], which keeps an open across a network disconnect. And not “safe in the bucket”: for the journal, durable means synced to its local device.

evict.name: evict
evict.short: To drop the local copy of bytes that are already offloaded. That alone frees no disk space: the space comes back when [[repack]] copies the segment's live records elsewhere and deletes it.
evict.long: Drop a local copy that is offloaded. Writes nothing to metadata and never touches the remote tier; frees no disk space by itself. The policy is the [[engine]]'s; the journal's mechanism for it is [[release]].

hole.name: hole
hole.short: A range below the file's size that was never written, or was deallocated. It reads as zeros without fetching anything.
hole.long: An extent of a file below its size that was never written, or was deallocated; it reads as zeros with no fetch. Metadata records it (RFC 6). The journal cannot tell a hole from an evicted or lost extent: it reports all three as [[missing]].

lost.name: Lost
lost.short: Said of bytes that were written but that nothing can serve any more. Reading them fails with an error; it never returns zeros.
lost.long: Said of bytes that were written, that no current chunk covers and the journal no longer holds, or whose block can no longer be decoded. Reading them fails; it never returns zeros.

write-verifier.name: write verifier
write-verifier.short: A value an NFS server returns with each write and commit. When it changes, the client resends the writes the server had not yet made stable.
write-verifier.long: The NFS value returned by a write and a commit (RFC 17 §5.8). It folds in the journal's [[loss-generation|loss generation]], so a journal that fails unsynced writes changes it, and clients resend those writes.

journal.name: journal
journal.short: The append-only store on a node's local disk where every write lands first, one per device. It keeps the bytes until they have been [[offload|offloaded]] to the [[remote-tier|remote tier]], and may keep them afterwards as a local copy.
journal.long: The local tier (RFC 1): an append-only store on a fast local disk, one per device, shared by every share placed on it. Writes are acknowledged from it. It holds extents of files and knows nothing of chunks, blocks or the remote tier.

record.name: record
record.short: One write as the journal stores it in a segment: a header with the write's identity, length and checksum, followed by its bytes.
record.long: One framed run of bytes within a [[segment]] — one write, or one piece of a write that crossed a segment's end — with a header carrying its identity, length and checksum (RFC 28 §2.3). Releases, removals and losses are recorded too, as header-only records.
record.clash: Not a [[metadata-record|metadata record]], which is one key and its value in the metadata store. And not a [[chunk]]: a record is whatever one write staged.

segment.name: segment
segment.short: An append-only journal file of records. It has a fixed size, is sealed when full, and its disk space comes back only when the whole segment is freed.
segment.long: A local append-only file of [[record|records]], capped at a fixed size (256 MiB in the RFC's examples) and sealed when full. Its space returns only when the whole segment is deleted or recycled as a spare: by [[repack]], after copying its live records forward, or by the journal itself once nothing in it is live.

held-extent.name: held extent
held-extent.short: An extent whose bytes the journal holds and can return, along with its content version and whether it has been offloaded.
held-extent.long: An extent of one file the journal holds and can produce, mapped to a place in a record, with its [[content-version]] and its [[offloaded-bit]]. A file's held extents are disjoint, and need not be adjacent nor start at offset zero.

offloaded-bit.name: offloaded bit
offloaded-bit.short: A mark per extent saying its bytes are already in the remote tier. The engine's [[report]] sets it after an upload, a [[fill]] sets it, since fetched bytes came from the remote tier, and `MarkOffloaded` sets it when the engine reseeds the bits after a restart. The journal releases nothing without it.
offloaded-bit.long: The journal's per-extent mark that it was told the bytes are offloaded; set by a [[report]], a [[fill]] or `MarkOffloaded`, and needed before [[release]]. Never consulted to answer a read. It can be wrong only in the safe direction: it can call offloaded bytes dirty, never dirty bytes offloaded.

offer.name: offer
offer.short: A frozen view of one file's dirty bytes that the journal hands the engine to upload. Writes made later do not change what the offer returns.
offer.long: The frozen view of dirty bytes the journal hands to an [[offload]]. A write during the pass changes what a read serves, not what the offer returns: the [[carver]] hashes the bytes and the uploader reads them again, and both must see the same ones.

report.name: report
report.short: The engine telling the journal which [[offer|offered]] extents are now offloaded. It is the only way the journal learns this.
report.long: The engine's statement of which extents of an [[offer]] are now offloaded, the only way the journal learns it. Made once per committed block while the offer runs; it marks exactly what it names, and never a newer write over it.

release.name: release
release.short: (journal) To stop holding extents that are offloaded; this is how eviction is carried out. It is refused for any extent that is not offloaded.
release.long: The journal's mechanism of [[evict|eviction]]; the policy is the engine's. Refused whole if any named extent's [[offloaded-bit]] is unset. It frees no storage: the bytes become [[unreclaimed-bytes|unreclaimed]] until their segment is retired.
release.clash: Dropping a whole file's content and records, once it has no name and no open, is also called a release: a [[file-release|file's release]]. The journal carries that out with its `Delete`, never with its `Release`, which is only eviction.

fill.name: fill
fill.short: Placing bytes fetched from the remote tier into the journal. A fill never writes over bytes the journal already holds.
fill.long: The only way an extent becomes held without a client write. It writes only where nothing is held, sets the [[offloaded-bit]], and is refused if the file's [[change-version]] moved since the read that found the gap.

repack.name: repack
repack.short: Copying the live records out of a mostly empty segment and then deleting the segment. It is the step that frees journal space.
repack.long: Copies a segment's still-live records into another segment, repoints the [[placement-index|index]] and unlinks the original. Local, discards nothing, keeps versions and offloaded bits, and prefers the segments with the least live payload. Unrelated to remote garbage collection (RFC 9).

unreclaimed-bytes.name: unreclaimed bytes
unreclaimed-bytes.short: Journal bytes still taking disk space although their extents were released or overwritten. Repack is what recovers that space.
unreclaimed-bytes.long: Journal bytes still allocated on disk whose extents were released or superseded, backing nothing. A full journal is usually short of space here, and only [[repack]] returns it.

loss-event.name: loss event
loss-event.short: An extent the journal stopped holding without being asked to, for example because it was corrupt or stale, or because its sync failed.
loss-event.long: An extent the journal stopped holding without being asked: dropped as corrupt, stale or superseded, acknowledged unreadable, failed with a sync window, or failed by a read-only journal. Each is counted and logged by the engine; nearly every one is also recorded as a loss record naming the exact record lost (a read-only journal can append none).

offload.name: offload
offload.short: The pass that copies a journal's dirty extents to the remote tier and records them in metadata.
offload.long: The pass that copies a journal's dirty extents to the remote tier and records them in metadata. The journal's side is to [[offer]] dirty extents and accept [[report|reports]]; it uploads nothing. Offload makes content evictable; [[release]] evicts it.
offload.clash: Not a client's flush (NFS `COMMIT`, SMB `FLUSH`, `fsync`), which only [[sync|syncs]] the journal and never waits for the bucket.

sync.name: sync
sync.short: To make records durable in the journal by forcing them onto the local device.
sync.long: Make durable in the journal. Every record is synced by the next `Sync` naming its file or within a fixed bound after the write (1 s proposed), whichever comes first. A client's flush waits for its records to be synced.
sync.clash: Content that has been [[offload|offloaded]] is also said to be “synced to the remote tier”, and the [[syncer]] moves blocks to the bucket. For the journal, sync means its local device only.

content-version.name: content version
content-version.short: A number that orders a file's writes and removals. Where two of them cover the same byte, the one with the higher number wins.
content-version.long: The number the journal assigns to each write, truncate, deallocate and delete, inside the file's serialised append. Unlike a [[sequence-number]] it keeps its meaning on another journal and in metadata. A fill carries the version of the [[ref]] it was fetched from.

change-version.name: change version
change-version.short: The highest content version among all the changes to a file's extents. A read returns it, and a later fill checks it to make sure the file has not changed since.
change-version.long: The highest content version of any operation that changed a file's extents: write, truncate, deallocate, delete, clone target. `ReadAt` returns it as `asOf`; a `Fill` with an older `asOf` writes nothing. A file with no entry is checked against one of 4,096 [[floor-bucket|floor buckets]].

removal-marker.name: removal marker
removal-marker.short: What a truncate, deallocate or delete leaves in the journal: the removed extent and the removal's version, with no bytes.
removal-marker.long: What a truncate, deallocate or delete leaves in the index: the removed extent and the removal's version, holding no bytes; content below that version is not held inside it. It lives until the engine settles it, after metadata records the removal, so a crash in between cannot lose it.

headroom.name: headroom
headroom.short: Space set aside outside every limit for the records that free space, such as releases, removals and seals. It lets a full journal still clean itself up.
headroom.long: Spare segments allocated in advance, outside every share's limit: room for header-only records (65,536 proposed, about 14 MiB) and a seal per stream, so a full journal can still release and remove. Below half of it, content writes and records that free nothing are refused.

missing.name: missing
missing.short: What a journal read reports for each part of the range it does not hold. The list is exact, and the caller's buffer is left untouched there.
missing.long: `ReadAt` names every sub-extent it does not hold in `missing` and leaves those bytes of the caller's buffer untouched: never zeros, never a short read, never widened to a segment or block. Never written, evicted and lost look the same; the engine tells them apart.

placement-index.name: placement index
placement-index.short: The journal's in-memory map from each file's offsets to the extents it holds. Every read consults it.
placement-index.long: Held in memory only and rebuilt at open from the segments. Per file, an ordered set (a B-tree, as the RFC advises) of disjoint held extents keyed by start offset, with versions, offloaded bits and removal markers. About 53–69 bytes per entry, under a configured bound that refuses writes.

append-stream.name: append stream
append-stream.short: One sequence of segments that records are appended to. Each stream syncs its own active segment.
append-stream.long: One sequence of segments that records are appended to, one active segment at a time; the stream count is configurable. The sync timer is per stream, and one sync covers every writer waiting on the stream (group commit).

share-tag.name: share tag
share-tag.short: A share's number within the installation. It is written into every record the share appends and is never reused.
share-tag.long: Minted from an [[installation]]-wide counter that is never lowered, and never 0, which marks the journal's own records. A file belongs to one tag for its life; a call through one share's handle on a file of another tag is refused with `ErrOtherShare`.

sequence-number.name: sequence number
sequence-number.short: The order in which this journal appended its records. The number means nothing outside this journal.
sequence-number.long: The order this journal appended its records in. Nearly every append takes a new one, a repack copy of content included; a record re-appended after a failed sync, or a header-only record that repack carries forward, keeps its own. It orders records at recovery; a read only checks it against the record it finds.

storage-binding.name: storage binding
storage-binding.short: The engine's entry for one share. It says where the share's data goes, through a handle on each journal and a flow to its remote store, and keeps the share's settings, health and budgets.
storage-binding.long: The engine's entry for one [[share]] (RFC 8 §2.3): its handle on each device [[journal]], the [[syncer]] flow to its [[remote-block-store]], its [[namespace]], its settings, health and budgets. Never stored.

stability-point.name: stability point
stability-point.short: A moment when a client asks for its data to be safe: a flush (NFS `COMMIT`, SMB `FLUSH`, `fsync`) or a stable write. The journal then syncs the file, and an overwrite of already committed content also waits until metadata has recorded it.
stability-point.long: Reaches the [[engine]] as `Commit`. The [[journal]] syncs the file; an overwrite of committed content also waits for its [[existence]] commit. Appends and hole fills are answered after the sync.
stability-point.clash: In the [[engine]], “commit” alone usually means a metadata transaction landing, such as an existence commit or an offload commit. NFS `COMMIT` is one kind of stability point, and the engine's method for all of them is also called `Commit`.

existence.name: existence
existence.short: The fact that a write happened: the file's size, its holes, which ranges were overwritten and its modification time. Metadata records it separately from the bytes, in a transaction called the existence commit.
existence.long: Recorded apart from the bytes: size, [[hole|holes]], the overwrite set and `mtime`. Committed across files in a [[group-commit]] within a bounded age (`existence_age`, proposal: 1 s). Until it is committed, the [[journal]] is its authority, and after a crash recovery re-applies it from the journal before the file is served.

group-commit.name: group commit
group-commit.short: One metadata transaction that records the pending existence of many files of one journal at once. It has a size limit, and it is split up when a file in it conflicts.
group-commit.long: Per [[journal]]: at most `G` files (proposal: 256) and the key budget `K` per transaction. A conflict delays only the failing file: retried alone at once when the store names the key, otherwise the batch is split in halves until it stands alone.
group-commit.clash: The [[metadata-store|metadata store]] uses the same name for sharing one device sync among several commits: see [[store-group-commit]].

residency.name: residency
residency.short: Where an extent's bytes are right now: Absent (a hole, read as zeros), [[dirty|Dirty]] (only in the journal), Resident (in the journal and uploaded), Remote (only in the bucket) or [[lost|Lost]]. The engine works it out on every read and never stores it.
residency.long: One of five classes (RFC 0 §4.2): **Absent** (a [[hole]] or a zero ref: zeros, no fetch), [[dirty|Dirty]] (only the journal holds it), **Resident** (held and offloaded), **Remote** (fetched and verified) and [[lost|Lost]] (written, and nowhere: the read fails). The [[engine]] computes it per request and keeps no copy.

ref.name: ref
ref.short: One file's use of one chunk at one offset. It names the chunk by its chunk ID, never by the block that contains it.
ref.long: One file's use of one [[chunk]] at one offset, with the versions it came from; it names the chunk by its chunk ID, never the [[block]] (RFC 0, RFC 6 §2.1). In the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] each ref is its own key (RFC 16 §1.2).

carved.name: hole / uncarved / carved
carved.short: Said of bytes already cut into chunks. For an offset below a file's size, metadata gives one of three answers: never written, written but not yet in any current chunk, or covered by a current chunk.
carved.long: Every offset below a file's size is in exactly one of three classes (RFC 6 §3.2). A [[hole]] was never written and reads as zeros. Uncarved bytes were written but are in no current chunk yet, so they exist only in a [[journal]]; if the journal no longer holds them, they are [[lost|Lost]]. Carved bytes are in a [[block]], so if no local copy is held they are fetched from the remote tier.

policy-component.name: policy component
policy-component.short: A small decision function in the engine, such as when to offload, whether to fill or what to evict. Whatever it decides, the mechanism it picks is safe on its own.
policy-component.long: RFC 8 defines five: `offloadDue`, `evict`, `repackDue`, `fill` and `admit`, plus a `health` struct. Each is a pure function, tested on its own with tables of cases. None of them may be the only thing standing between the system and data loss.

work-queue.name: work queue
work-queue.short: An in-memory queue, one per device journal, that turns events into work: offload passes, batches of removals, and prunes of a file's superseded overwrite records.
work-queue.long: Fed by `Dirty` events, the age tick, capacity pressure and pending removals, and fair between [[share|shares]] by budget. Posting never blocks, one key is in at most one run, and nothing is stored: it is rebuilt from the [[journal]], the [[put-intent|put intents]] and the metadata records whenever the node gains a shard.

offload-pipeline.name: offload pipeline
offload-pipeline.short: The state machine that runs one offload pass. It captures the offer, carves it into chunks, assembles blocks, writes a put intent, uploads, commits, and marks the bytes offloaded.
offload-pipeline.long: Every step has a deadline and says what happens when it fails. Every failure ends with the extent either [[report|reported]] offloaded or [[dirty|Dirty]] with its file retried later, and retries never stop while the node is the shard's [[primary]]. It holds no bytes and persists nothing.

offload-guard.name: offload guard
offload-guard.short: A short lock on one file, held only while an offer is captured and while a commit runs, never during the upload.
offload-guard.long: Removals hold it across their journal step and their first metadata transaction, so no [[offer]] is captured between the two. It is an optimisation, not a fence: what orders commits is the [[metadata-store]]'s conflict on the file's fence records, and correctness must not depend on the guard.
offload-guard.clash: Not the metadata store's [[guard]], a transaction's claim on a key it does not write, which aborts its own transaction if that key changed.

put-intent.name: put intent
put-intent.short: A durable note, written before every upload, that names the block about to be uploaded. The commit that records the block deletes the note.
put-intent.long: Carries the [[block-name]] and the epochs the pass runs under. If the commit never lands, the uploaded object is an orphan — leaked space, not lost content — that GC reclaims through its intent.

block-name.name: block name
block-name.short: A block's 32-byte identity. Each upload attempt mints a new one, which a retry inside that attempt keeps; a name is never used by a second attempt.
block-name.long: A hash of a domain, the [[namespace]], a fresh 16-byte nonce, the chain ID and the ordered chunk hashes. A retry within one attempt reuses it; a new attempt mints a new one, even over identical chunks.

speculator.name: speculator
speculator.short: The engine module that plans fetches nobody has asked for yet: read-ahead for sequential readers, and pre-warm of files an operator names.
speculator.long: It plans; the [[syncer]]'s fetcher executes. It never delays a demand read, never causes a write to be refused, and never fetches a block the [[journal]] holds whole.

pacing.name: pacing
pacing.short: Slowing writes down gradually once dirty and [[unreclaimed-bytes|unreclaimed]] bytes pass half of the journal's limit, instead of stopping them all at once at the limit.
pacing.long: The delay rises in a straight line, from zero at half the limit to the time the journal takes to drain the write at the limit. Clean held bytes do not count. A delay that would pass the caller's deadline returns [[retry-later]] at once.

self-fence.name: self-fence
self-fence.short: What the engine does when a metadata write transaction has been pending or failing for 30 s and none has committed: it answers writes and flushes with retry-later and keeps serving reads.
self-fence.long: The 30 s are measured on the node's one clock. While fenced, writes and [[stability-point|stability points]] are answered [[retry-later]], reads continue, and a health condition names the store at fault. The fence lifts on the next successful commit, or once no write transaction is outstanding or failing.

loss-generation.name: loss generation
loss-generation.short: A counter in each journal that rises only on [[loss-event|loss events]]. It is folded into the NFS write verifier.
loss-generation.long: Monotonic for the life of the process, across reopens of the [[journal]]. When it rises, the [[write-verifier]] changes and clients resend their unstable writes. A loss of content the [[remote-tier]] already holds makes no client resend.

metadata-store.name: metadata store
metadata-store.short: The one transactional database that holds every fact DittoFS remembers, except the bytes of files.
metadata-store.long: The transactional store holding every fact about files, content, identity and configuration (RFC 0). It sits behind the [[kv|KV]]: an embedded store on one node, a replicated one in a cluster (RFC 16).

namespace.name: namespace
namespace.short: One prefix, like a folder, inside a bucket of the remote tier. Chunks are named and counted within one namespace, never across two.
namespace.long: One prefix, like a folder, inside a bucket of the [[remote-tier|remote tier]]: [[chunk|chunks]] are named and counted within it, never across two. Each [[share]] gets its own by default; a clone or a restore joins its source's, and during a re-home a share has two.
namespace.clash: Two other things share the word. The metadata store's `Namespace` [[view]] is its interface for names and directories, and namespace metadata is the file tree itself: names, directories, attributes. NFSv4 calls the tree joining every export the pseudo-filesystem namespace. None of them is a bucket prefix.

remote-block-store.name: remote block store
remote-block-store.short: The adapter for one remote-tier backend, such as S3 or memory. It maps block names to object keys and makes exactly one attempt per call.
remote-block-store.long: Every [[share]] has one: RFC 8 refuses to add a share whose configuration names none, so an [[offload]] always has a target. A deployment that wants no remote service configures a remote block store of its own.

shard.name: shard
shard.short: A set of files served by one primary at a time. A share is one shard; only in a cluster can part of a share be a shard of its own.
shard.long: A set of files with one [[primary]] at a time. A [[share]] is one shard, and only in a cluster can a subtree, or each child of a marked directory, be its own. A file is never split across shards (RFC 0, RFC 11 §2). Shard numbers are installation-wide and never reused (RFC 16 §2.3.1).

shard-incarnation.name: shard incarnation
shard-incarnation.short: A number in the shard record, raised each time a node or a journal begins serving the shard as primary: every node start and every journal attach, though not an in-place reopen.
shard-incarnation.long: A number in the shard record raised each time a node or a journal begins serving the shard as [[primary]]: every node start, a re-claim and every journal attach, though not an in-place reopen of the journal. It fences nothing; it feeds the [[write-verifier|write verifier]] and names the [[grace-instance]].

client-id.name: client (client ID)
client-id.short: One running client machine or process, as the server knows it. A client that reboots gets a new client ID.
client-id.long: One running client machine or process, as the server knows it, holding opens, locks and grants. Found again by its own name; a reboot makes a new client ID. An SMB record names a machine, not a user.

open.name: open
open.short: One open of one file by a client. It records the access the client was granted and the access it denies to others.
open.long: One open of one file by a client: the access granted (read, write, delete) and the access it denies to every other open. NFSv3 has none and uses an [[anonymous-open]]. An open keeps a file alive.

lock-owner.name: lock owner
lock-owner.short: Whoever holds a byte-range lock. Depending on the protocol, that is a process, an open or a whole host.
lock-owner.long: Who holds a [[byte-range-lock]]: a name the client picks (a process) in NFSv4, each open in SMB, a host in NLM. Two owners of one client conflict as two clients would.

byte-range-lock.name: byte-range lock
byte-range-lock.short: A lock on a range of a file, held by a lock owner. SMB locks are mandatory, NFS locks advisory.
byte-range-lock.long: A lock on a range [offset, last] of a file, over 64 bits, held by a [[lock-owner]]. SMB locks are mandatory: they refuse the reads and writes across their range that the lock forbids. NFS locks are advisory: they refuse only other locks.

lock-waiter.name: lock waiter
lock-waiter.short: A lock request waiting for a range to become free. The primary records it instead of keeping a worker busy waiting.
lock-waiter.long: A lock request that conflicted with a held lock and asked to wait. The [[primary]] records it and answers at once. When the range frees, waiters are served first in, first out: a poll waiter gets the freed range reserved for it, and a callback waiter is granted the lock by the server.

state-reference.name: state reference
state-reference.short: The ID a client presents to name one open, lock state or caching grant: a stateid in NFSv4, a FileId in SMB.
state-reference.long: The ID a client presents for an open, a lock state or a [[caching-grant]]: a stateid in NFSv4, a `FileId` in SMB. Resolved only at the [[primary]]; it carries bits of its [[grace-instance]].

open-state-step.name: open-state step
open-state-step.short: The per-file order in which calls that use open state run, one at a time. Each call holds the file's [[admission-lock|admission lock]] across its check and the I/O that check allows.
open-state-step.long: The per-file serialisation of every open-state call: the service's [[admission-lock|admission lock]], held across a check and the I/O it admits, then the table's entry mutex. A step decides, persists, then applies.

client-lease.name: client lease
client-lease.short: How long the server keeps the state of a client it no longer hears from: 90 s, renewed by every request. Not every client has one: an NLM host has none.
client-lease.long: How long the server keeps a silent client's state: 90 s, fixed, renewed by every request. Silent for a whole period, the client is gone and all it held is released. Not every client has one: an NLM host has none, and an SMB-durable open's `Timeout` plays that part for a client without one. Not a node lease, nor an SMB [[lease]].

lease-owner.name: lease owner
lease-owner.short: (cluster) The one node that renews a client's [[client-lease|lease]] and decides when the client has expired. No primary expires a client on its own.
lease-owner.long: (cluster) The one node that renews and expires a [[client-id|client]]. Serving nodes report the client's activity to it at most once per renewal interval, 10 s (proposed); no [[primary]] expires a client alone.

grace-period.name: grace period
grace-period.short: A window after a primary loses its open state. During it, only clients that held state before may take state, and only by reclaiming what they had. Other requests for state get `ErrGrace`.
grace-period.long: A window that opens after a [[primary]] loses its open state and lasts one [[client-lease|lease period]], 90 s. During it the primary refuses new open state and accepts only reclaims from clients it has a record of. It ends on its own, or early once all those clients have finished reclaiming.
grace-period.clash: Not the trash where garbage collection keeps blocks for a while before deleting them, which is no grace period, and not the narrower grace that a [[namespace-move|namespace move]] runs.

grace-instance.name: grace instance
grace-instance.short: One grace period of one shard. Every loss of the shard's open state starts a new one.
grace-instance.long: One grace period of one [[shard]]. Each loss of its open state sets the instance to the current [[shard-incarnation]]; a handover that ships the table keeps it.

open-reclaim.name: reclaim (open state)
open-reclaim.short: A client, during the grace period, taking back the opens, locks and grants it held before the loss, and never more than that.
open-reclaim.long: During [[grace-period|grace]], a client taking back what it held: only if its durable record names the shard, never more than it held, after the permission checks of a new open. Two conflicting reclaims never both hold.
open-reclaim.clash: Not the journal's reclaim, which gets back local disk space without changing any content.

recall.name: recall
recall.short: The server taking back a caching grant because another client's request conflicts with it. SMB calls it a break.
recall.long: Taking back a [[caching-grant]] because another client's request conflicts; SMB calls it a break. The holder flushes and acknowledges. Deadline: 35 s for a grant that covers opens, 90 s for one that covers none.

delegation.name: delegation
delegation.short: NFSv4's caching grant, for reading or for reading and writing. It is offered only to a client whose callback channel works.
delegation.long: NFSv4's [[caching-grant]]: read, or write (read and write). The server may offer one in the `OPEN` reply when it sees no conflict and the client has a working callback channel. It covers no open: an unanswered [[recall]] revokes it at 90 s.

oplock.name: oplock
oplock.short: SMB's older caching promise, held by one open. It comes in three levels: Level II (read), exclusive (read and write) and batch (read, write and [[handle-caching|handle caching]]).
oplock.long: An opportunistic lock: a [[caching-grant]] held by one open. Level II is read, exclusive is read and write, batch is read, write and handle. Keyed by its open, so two opens of one client break each other, as oplocks always have. Since SMB 2.1 a client may ask for a lease instead.

revoked-set.name: revoked set
revoked-set.short: For each client, the references a primary has revoked. Every use of one is answered ErrRevoked until the client frees it.
revoked-set.long: Per client and [[primary]], the [[state-reference|references]] the server revoked. Each is answered `ErrRevoked` until the client frees it with `FreeState`; renewals carry a flag meanwhile. Volatile.

grant-budget.name: grant budget
grant-budget.short: Each primary gives one client at most 4,096 caching grants. At that number the client is offered no new grant and, where its protocol can ask, is asked to give grants back down to 2,048.
grant-budget.long: Each [[primary]] keeps a client's caching grants within 4,096. At the budget no new grant is offered and, where the protocol allows, the client is asked to return grants down to 2,048. Volatile.

delete-pending.name: delete pending
delete-pending.short: SMB's delete on close. The name stays until the last open closes, and new opens are refused in the meantime.
delete-pending.long: SMB's delete on close: the name stays until the last open closes, and new opens of either protocol are refused. The last close removes the name as the [[principal]] that marked it.

smb-durable-open.name: SMB-durable open
smb-durable-open.short: An SMB open kept across a network disconnect until its timeout. It lives in memory only, so it does not survive a restart of its primary.
smb-durable-open.long: An SMB open kept across a lost connection for the `Timeout` it negotiated, with its locks, deny mode and lease. It lives only in the [[primary|primary's]] memory: a restart or failover loses it.
smb-durable-open.clash: SMB's "durable" means kept across a disconnect, in memory. For open state, durable means written to the [[metadata-store|metadata store]], and for the journal it means synced to the journal's device. Of SMB's opens, only a [[persistent-open]] is written to the metadata store.

persistent-open.name: persistent open
persistent-open.short: An SMB open that also survives a restart or failover of its primary, because it is written to the metadata store.
persistent-open.long: An SMB open that survives a disconnect for its `Timeout` (up to 300 s) and a restart or failover of its [[primary]]: it has a durable record, and its writes are stable. Opt-in per share, off by default.

nlm.name: NLM / NSM
nlm.short: NFSv3's lock protocol, together with its companion protocol for restart notices. NLM locks have no lease.
nlm.long: NLM is NFSv3's lock protocol. It has no lease: a host's locks last until it unlocks them or restarts. NSM carries restart notices; a durable NSM state number rises when a failover loses NLM locks.

watch.name: watch
watch.short: A client's request to be told when a directory changes. It lives in memory only, and a client cannot reclaim it after the server loses it.
watch.long: A request to be told when a directory changes, such as SMB's change notify. At most 1,024 per client per [[primary]], 64 changes each before collapsing to 'enumerate directory' (both proposed). Volatile, never reclaimed.

installation.name: installation
installation.short: All the nodes that share one metadata store and control plane. The first release's installation is one node.
installation.long: All the [[node|nodes]] that share one [[metadata-store|metadata store]] and control plane; the widest scope a setting has. The first release's installation is one node (RFC 0, RFC 13 §3). Its identity is one record, written once by the explicit initialisation step (RFC 16 §2.3).

snapshot.name: snapshot (share)
snapshot.short: The share as it was at one cut, read-only. A cut is a number marking one instant of a share.
snapshot.long: A cut is a number marking one instant of a [[share]], raised by one at each snapshot; snapshot k is the share as it was when its cut number became k, read-only (RFC 0, RFC 12 §2.2).
snapshot.clash: A [[kv|KV]] transaction also runs “against one snapshot”: the consistent view of the whole store it reads from. That is not a share snapshot.

gc.name: GC
gc.short: Garbage collection. It retires blocks that nothing references, keeps them in a trash for a while, then deletes them, and it compacts blocks that are mostly dead.
gc.long: The component that retires, holds in trash and deletes [[block|blocks]] nothing references, and compacts mostly-dead ones (RFC 0, RFC 9). It holds one [[view]] of the metadata store, `Blocks`.

fence-records.name: fence records
fence-records.short: Two records per file holding the shard and its [[epoch|shard epoch]] that the file's commits must carry, one for the existence path and one for the offload path. Every commit checks its path's record; only commits that must exclude each other write it.
fence-records.long: Two records per file, `F_x` for the existence path and `F_o` for the offload path, each holding the (shard, epoch) its commits must carry. Every commit [[guard|guards]] its path's fence, so it fails if the epoch moved. Only commits that must exclude each other write it: a primary under a new epoch, removals and releases, and, for `F_o`, every offload commit. On a single node only the epoch comparison is moot (RFC 0, RFC 6 §5.4).

entity.name: entity
entity.short: A plain value a read returns, such as a File, an Entry or a Share. One entity is not one stored record.
entity.long: A plain value a metadata read returns, such as a File, an Entry or a Share; not one stored [[metadata-record|record]] (RFC 0). What a write touches is decided by the operation, never by the struct (RFC 16 §1.2).

metadata-record.name: record (metadata)
metadata-record.short: One key and its value in the [[kv|KV]]. Every key the metadata store writes is listed, with its layout, in the store's one table of keys.
metadata-record.long: One key and its value in the [[kv|KV]]. Every key the store writes has a row in RFC 16's key table, which is exhaustive: a new record kind is a format bump (§4.2).
metadata-record.clash: Not a journal [[record]], which is one write as stored in a segment. And not an [[entity]]: one entity may be read from several records.

kv.name: KV
kv.short: The small interface a metadata backend implements. It runs a transaction, and inside it reads, scans, sets, deletes and guards keys.
kv.long: The small interface a metadata backend implements (RFC 0): `Update`, `View` and `Limits`, and inside a transaction reads, scans, writes, guards and `Now`. The entity layer is written once over it (RFC 16 §4.1).

guard.name: guard
guard.short: A transaction's claim on a key it does not write: it aborts its own transaction if the key changed since its snapshot.
guard.long: A transaction's claim on a key it does not write, or on every key under a prefix (a range guard). It aborts its own transaction if the key was written after that transaction's snapshot; it never stops the writer, and never conflicts with another guard (RFC 0, RFC 16 §4.1).

delta-fold.name: delta and fold
delta-fold.short: How a counter that many writers change is updated. It is never read and rewritten: each transaction adds a separate delta record, and the deltas are folded into the total later.
delta-fold.long: A counter many writers change — usage, a directory's times — is never read and rewritten. Each transaction writes a delta under a key of its own; the [[primary]] of the [[shard]] folds them later: usage into per-shard totals, times into the directory's record (RFC 16 §4.4).
delta-fold.clash: Not a name's case fold, which a [[fold-rule|fold rule]] decides: same word, unrelated mechanism.

fold-rule.name: fold rule
fold-rule.short: How a share turns a name into its key: unchanged on a case-sensitive share, through a fixed upcase table otherwise.
fold-rule.long: How a [[share]] turns a file name into its entry's key: unchanged on a case-sensitive share, through a fixed 16-bit upcase table otherwise. Recorded by ID in the [[format-record|format record]] (RFC 16 §4.6, RFC 7 §3.3).
fold-rule.clash: Not the [[delta-fold|fold]] that merges counter deltas into totals.

view.name: view
view.short: The narrow interface one consumer is handed: the engine, GC and the filesystem service each hold different ones.
view.long: The narrow interface one consumer of the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] is handed. Interfaces follow consumers, not entities: there is no per-entity CRUD interface. Adapters hold none of them, only `vfs.Service` (RFC 16 §1.2, §3).

format-record.name: format record
format-record.short: The one record the store reads first. It holds the store format and each share's fold rule, and a binary that does not know them refuses to open the store.
format-record.long: The record `\x00format`, read before any other key: the store format and the shares' [[fold-rule|fold rules]]. Only the control plane's gate raises it, never the opening of a store (RFC 16 §4.6).

store-group-commit.name: group commit (store)
store-group-commit.short: Commits that are ready at the same time share one sync of the device. None of them is acknowledged before that sync completes.
store-group-commit.long: Commits ready at the same moment share one sync of the device, and none is acknowledged before it. The embedded backend does it, because one sync per commit would cap a store at a few hundred commits a second.
store-group-commit.clash: Not the [[engine]]'s [[group-commit]], which batches many files' existence into one metadata transaction. This one shares a device sync among commits.

store-time.name: store time (Now)
store-time.short: The time a transaction reads from the store. It never goes backwards from one commit to the next (on a store without a timestamp oracle, a service that hands out ordered commit times, only within one node), and stays within a stated bound of real time.
store-time.long: The time `Now` gives a transaction, used for every stored time compared later. Monotonic across commits in order, within a stated bound of real time; across nodes on a store without an oracle, readings may differ by up to σ (RFC 16 §4.1).

value-codec.name: codec (store)
value-codec.short: How one stored type is encoded: a version byte, then the fields in a fixed order. A version the binary does not know is refused, never guessed.
value-codec.long: One per persisted type: a version byte, then a fixed field order. A binary writes only the versions the active format names, and refuses an unknown one rather than guess (RFC 16 §4.3).
value-codec.clash: Not an [[adapter]]'s [[codec]], which turns wire bytes into a request's fields.

principal.name: principal
principal.short: A protocol-neutral identity: a user, a group, a machine or a well-known principal. Its ID is never reissued to anyone else.
principal.long: A user, group, machine or well-known principal. Its ID is minted at creation and never reissued — a well-known one has a fixed ID — so a reused UID or SID inherits nothing. Protocol spellings live only on the User or Group record (RFC 16 §2.2, RFC 18).

change-sequence.name: change sequence
change-sequence.short: The version the store gives a write when it commits. Writes are ordered by it exactly as their commits are.
change-sequence.long: The version the store assigns at commit, so it orders writes like their commits; no transaction writes a counter to get it. A key the transaction itself wrote has none yet (RFC 16 §4.1).

key-budget.name: key budget (K)
key-budget.short: How many items, conflict ranges included, one transaction may carry when an operation over many refs, such as a removal, is split into batches. It is derived from the backend's limits.
key-budget.long: The most items one batch transaction may carry, owned by RFC 6 and derived from `Limits`: a transaction's largest key and value, bytes, entries and age — backend properties, never settings (RFC 16 §4.1).

inspect.name: Inspect
inspect.short: A view that reads by ID without checking permissions. It is for trusted internal consumers only and is never handed to an adapter.
inspect.long: A [[view]] that reads files, entries, ACLs, refs, chunks and blocks by ID, without authorisation, for trusted internal consumers. Handed to an adapter, it would bypass the permission [[chokepoint]] (RFC 16 §3.1).

vfs-filesystem.name: filesystem (*vfs.Filesystem)
vfs-filesystem.short: The implementation of the filesystem service that decides every call, at the file's primary.
vfs-filesystem.long: The implementation of the [[filesystem-service]] that decides: it runs [[admission]], authorisation, the open-state check, quota and the [[engine]] call, in one order, at the file's [[primary]]. On a single node the adapters call it directly; in a cluster they call a gateway.
vfs-filesystem.clash: Not a filesystem in the kernel sense (ext4, XFS), and not the Linux kernel's VFS layer, which share only the idea. In the filesystem service, "filesystem" with no qualifier means this type.

chokepoint.name: chokepoint
chokepoint.short: The one function in the metadata store that decides file permissions; the service is its only caller.
chokepoint.long: The one function in the metadata store that decides file permissions (`Files.Authorize`, with `Files.Granted`). The service's `authz` package is its only caller, and the service never evaluates a permission itself.

share-grant.name: share grant
share-grant.short: One principal's access to one share: none, read, read-write or admin. It is checked on every call.
share-grant.long: One principal's access to one share (none, read, read-write, admin), read at [[admission]] on every call and applied as a ceiling before the file's mode or ACL. Not the export policy. Removing it takes effect on the next call.
share-grant.clash: Not a [[caching-grant]] (a lease or delegation), and not an open's open-time grant, the access recorded when an open was granted. All three are called "grant".

pseudo-filesystem.name: pseudo-filesystem
pseudo-filesystem.short: The read-only tree of directories through which an NFSv4 client reaches each share's root.
pseudo-filesystem.long: The read-only tree of directories through which an NFSv4 client reaches each share's root. Built by the service from the share list, the same on every node, and showing only paths to shares the caller would be admitted to.

route-envelope.name: route envelope
route-envelope.short: (cluster) The routing information every forwarded call carries: the request ID, the shard and its [[epoch]], the sending node and its [[node-epoch|node epoch]], and a hop count.
route-envelope.long: (cluster) What every call the gateway forwards carries: the request ID, the shard and its epoch, the sending node and its node epoch, and a hop count. `Serve` at the primary fences on it and answers a retry from its dedup table.

lock-order.name: lock order
lock-order.short: The one order in which every call takes its locks, so no two calls wait on each other forever. First the [[admission-lock|admission lock]] of each file it touches, then [[fold-admission|fold admission]] at each directory it changes, then the [[accept-lock|accept lock]] of each file it changes.
lock-order.long: The one order every call takes what it needs: the [[admission-lock|admission lock]] of each file it touches, then [[fold-admission|fold admission]] at the directories it changes, then the [[accept-lock|accept locks]] of the files it draws for — each in file-ID order. So no two calls each hold what the other waits for.

wcc.name: WCC
wcc.short: Weak cache consistency: one object's attributes just before and just after a change, captured together with the change itself.
wcc.long: A pair `{Before, After}`: one object's attributes on either side of a change, read during a single hold of the file's [[accept-lock|accept lock]]. Every call that changes something returns it, so no adapter has to follow a change with a separate `GetAttr`. `Before` may be absent where it cannot be read atomically.

quota-reservation.name: quota reservation
quota-reservation.short: Bytes or inodes a call sets aside against every quota before it changes anything. The reservation is released when the commit recording its charge lands, or when the call fails.
quota-reservation.long: What a write, a create or a copy sets aside against each quota scope before anything changes: the bytes it adds, or one inode. Held in the primary's memory, and released exactly once, however its bytes end (committed, committed from a loss record, or dropped), or when the call fails.

file-release.name: release (of a file)
file-release.short: Dropping a file's content and records once it has no name left and no open.
file-release.long: Dropping a file's refs, its journal content and its records once it has no name and no open. The service runs every one, at the file's primary, through the engine's `Delete`; a pending-release record makes a crash in between leak nothing.
file-release.clash: Not the [[journal]]'s own [[release]], which only stops holding offloaded extents and is the mechanism of eviction.

dialect.name: dialect
dialect.short: The SMB version a connection agrees on when it negotiates. DittoFS serves 2.1, 3.0, 3.0.2 and 3.1.1.
dialect.long: The protocol version a connection agrees in `NEGOTIATE`: the highest of 3.1.1, 3.0.2, 3.0 and 2.1 that the client offers. SMB1 and SMB 2.0.2 are refused.

credit.name: credit
credit.short: SMB's flow control. Each request spends credits and each response grants some back; DittoFS aims at 512 per connection.
credit.long: SMB's [[flow-control]]: a request costs one credit per 64 KiB and each response grants some back, so the credits a client holds bound what it has in flight. Kept per connection in the [[gateway-node|gateway node's]] memory; never revoked once granted.

signing.name: signing
signing.short: Every SMB message after sign-in carries a signature made with the session's key. DittoFS requires it on every session except the keyless null and guest ones.
signing.long: Each message after session setup carries a signature made with the [[session|session's]] key. Every `NEGOTIATE` response requires it; a request neither signed nor encrypted is refused. Only keyless null and guest sessions are exempt.

tree-connect.name: tree connect
tree-connect.short: An SMB session's attachment to one share. It lives in one node's memory and is never stored.
tree-connect.long: `TREE_CONNECT` attaches a [[session]] to one [[share]]; its reply carries the share's flags. Like the session, it lives in one [[gateway-node|gateway node's]] memory and is never stored.

ipc.name: IPC$
ipc.short: Not a file share: it is the SMB adapter's RPC endpoint, used to list shares and look up names. It reaches no file.
ipc.long: A tree that reaches no file: named pipes for exactly three DCE/[[rpc|RPC]] services — srvsvc (share lists), wkssvc and lsarpc (security identifiers to names). Every other call is refused. It is all a null session may reach.

file-id.name: FileId (SMB)
file-id.short: The number that names one SMB open on the wire. Its persistent half is valid on any node; its volatile half only on the node that issued it.
file-id.long: Names an open, not a file. Its persistent half is derived from the [[open-state]] open's ID and names its shard, so any node can route a reconnect to the open's [[primary]]. Its volatile half names an entry in the gateway node's table and is invalid on any other node.
file-id.clash: Not the internal ID that names a file inside DittoFS, which a file [[handle]] carries and which never reaches the SMB wire, nor the numeric file id Windows is shown. And not an NFS file handle, which names a file, not an open.

lease-break.name: break
lease-break.short: The server taking back an SMB lease or oplock. The holder flushes its data and acknowledges, while the conflicting request waits.
lease-break.long: The primary taking a [[lease]] or [[oplock]] back when a request conflicts with it. Breaking write or handle caching needs an acknowledgement; the waiting request holds no worker. At its 35 s deadline the grant drops to none, and no open closes.

caching-fence.name: caching fence
caching-fence.short: After a lease break times out, that primary offers the client machine no new lease or oplock for 90 s.
caching-fence.long: After a [[lease-break|break]] times out, the whole machine — one [[client-guid|ClientGuid]] — is offered no new lease or oplock for 90 s at that primary; each further timeout restarts the period. Its opens stay open.

durable-handle.name: durable handle
durable-handle.short: An SMB open that outlives a lost connection until a timeout, 60 s by default and at most 300 s. It does not survive the loss of its primary.
durable-handle.long: An SMB open kept across a network disconnect for its timeout, held in the [[primary|primary's]] memory: a planned handover carries it; a restart or failover of the primary does not, and its reconnect is then refused.
durable-handle.clash: Not **durable** in the journal's sense, data synced to the journal's disk: on a share that is not continuously available, writes through a durable handle may not be synced yet.

persistent-handle.name: persistent handle
persistent-handle.short: A durable handle that is also stored, so it survives the loss of its primary. It is offered only on continuously available shares.
persistent-handle.long: An SMB open that also survives a restart or failover of its [[primary]], because it is stored; every write through it is synced before it is acknowledged. Granted only on a [[continuously-available]] share.

continuously-available.name: continuously available (CA)
continuously-available.short: A share setting that promises handles outlive the loss of a server. On such a share DittoFS grants persistent handles and makes every write stable, and in a cluster it also serves Witness.
continuously-available.long: A [[share]] marked continuously available says so to SMB 3.x clients at tree connect. There [[persistent-handle|persistent handles]] are granted, and every write on the share, through any open, is synced before it is acknowledged. In a cluster [[witness|Witness]] is served too; a single node serves none.

client-guid.name: ClientGuid
client-guid.short: The ID one Windows machine sends on every connection. DittoFS keeps one client record per ClientGuid, tied to no particular user.
client-guid.long: SMB names a client by its `ClientGuid`, the same on every connection of one machine, even a host carrying many users. So there is one [[open-state]] client record per machine, and who may use an open is checked against the open's principal.

channel-sequence.name: channel sequence
channel-sequence.short: A counter kept with each SMB 3.x open, so the primary can refuse a stale or duplicate WRITE, SET_INFO or IOCTL.
channel-sequence.long: Kept with the open at the primary (`Channel.Seq`) with counts of the requests in flight, and checked as MS-SMB2 3.3.5.2.10 says, so a replay never runs beside its original. A persistent open stores it.

witness.name: Witness
witness.short: (cluster) The SMB service that tells a client of a continuously available share which server addresses are up, and asks it to move before a node drains.
witness.long: (cluster) MS-SWN, served by every gateway node for continuously available shares: it lists the floating addresses and sends `RESOURCE_CHANGE`, `CLIENT_MOVE` and `IP_CHANGE`, so a client reconnects at once. Registrations are not stored.

private-use-mapping.name: private-use mapping
private-use-mapping.short: How a name holding a character Windows reserves is shown over SMB: each such character becomes a fixed private-use code point.
private-use-mapping.long: On a `posix` share, each character Windows reserves in a stored name — `" * : < > ? \ |`, a control character, a trailing space or period — is shown as a code point from U+F001 to U+F029 (`:` is U+F022), and mapped back on the way in.

dt.name: dt
dt.short: The one command that runs every DittoFS test suite the same way, on a laptop or in CI. Written in Go.
dt.long: The one entry point, `test/harness/bin/dt`, built from `cmd/dt`. It reads the [[registry]], plans [[cell|cells]], sets up each [[fixture]], calls the test tool directly, [[grade|grades]] the results and writes them.

registry.name: registry
registry.short: `test/suites.yaml`: the one file that lists every suite, with its options and groups.
registry.long: `test/suites.yaml`, the one file listing every [[suite]] with its [[suite-option|options]] and [[suite-group|groups]], in a specified YAML format. `dt` refuses a file that doesn't match it. Tests aren't listed: each suite finds its own.

suite.name: suite
suite.short: A command that runs many tests, such as pjdfstest or the Go unit tests. `test/suites.yaml` lists every one.
suite.long: A command that runs many tests: `go test`, pjdfstest through `prove`, pynfs, smbtorture, the system scenarios. The suite finds its own tests, so adding a test is adding a file, not a line in the [[registry]].

suite-option.name: option
suite-option.short: A variant of a suite, run as `dt run SUITE --OPTION`, instead of a suite of its own.
suite-option.long: A named variant of a [[suite]], such as `integration --kerberos` or `unit --windows`: a copy of the suite with each field it sets replaced as a whole. It runs as its own [[cell|cells]].

suite-group.name: group
suite-group.short: A name for a set of suites run together, such as `conformance` or `lint`.
suite-group.long: A name for a set of [[suite|suites]]: `dt run conformance` runs pjdfstest, pynfs, WPTS and smbtorture. Groups for components (`journal`, `syncer`, `engine`) are added as each gets a suite of its own.

cell.name: cell
cell.short: One unit of a test run: a suite, or one of its options, at one combination of the values in its [[matrix]].
cell.long: What `dt plan` makes of a [[suite]]: one per combination of its [[matrix]] values, and per [[test-shard]], such as `pjdfstest/badger-s3/4.1`. Each has its own [[fixture]], results, exit status and CI job.

matrix.name: matrix
matrix.short: The axes a suite runs over, such as profile and NFS version: one cell per combination.
matrix.long: The axes and values a [[suite]] runs over. pjdfstest's `{ profile: [badger-s3], nfs: ["3", "4", "4.1"] }` makes three [[cell|cells]]. An axis no command, fixture or variable uses is refused.

test-shard.name: shard
test-shard.short: A slice of a cell's tests, run in a CI job of its own to finish sooner.
test-shard.long: A slice of a [[cell]]'s tests in a CI job of its own, the tests dealt in turn so long and short ones spread evenly. smbtorture runs on two shards, in every [[tier]].
test-shard.clash: Not a storage [[shard]], a set of files with one primary. Here a shard is a slice of a test run.

store-profile.name: store profile
store-profile.short: The stores a test server runs on: `memory`, `badger` or `badger-s3`, the one production uses.
store-profile.long: The stores a [[fixture]]'s server uses: `memory`, `badger` or `badger-s3`. Conformance runs `badger-s3` only, the production profile. For an S3 profile `dt` creates the bucket and checks it takes a write and a read.
store-profile.clash: Not a performance profile (pprof), nor the coverage profile the unit suite writes: a store profile names the stores a test server runs on.

fixture.name: fixture
fixture.short: The DittoFS server a suite's tests run against, built and checked by `dt` before the first test.
fixture.long: `dfs` built from the checkout, on a [[store-profile|store profile]], with its [[share|shares]] and users, mounted when the suite needs it. `dt` sets it up from the suite's fields (no setup script), checks it, and removes it after the last test.
fixture.clash: In Go or pytest a fixture is a small piece of test setup, such as a file under `testdata`. In the test harness it is a whole running server, with stores, shares, users and a mount.

needs.name: needs
needs.short: What a machine must offer to run a suite: Linux, root, Docker, a service, free disk.
