needs.long: What a [[suite]] requires: a platform, `root` (passwordless sudo), a container engine, tools, `disk:<GB>`, `port:<n>`, `host:dedicated`, `service:<name>`. `dt doctor` says which are met; unless `dtc` meets it, an unmet one is [[not-run|not run]], never passed.

dedicated-host.name: dedicated host
dedicated-host.short: `ditto`, a large test server that runs the long and disk-hungry suites. Not a GitHub runner.
dedicated-host.long: `ditto`, a server Cubbit rents, which runs from cron the [[cell|cells]] hosted runners can't hold: the system scenarios, the long runs, the performance night. It is not a self-hosted runner, and its token writes only issues and commit statuses.

tier.name: tier
tier.short: When a suite runs: `pr` on every pull request, `merge` after each merge, `nightly`, or `manual`.
tier.long: The set of [[suite|suites]] a run includes, by when it runs: `pr` (p90 ≤ 20 min), `merge` (≤ 60 min), `nightly` (≤ 4 h), `manual`. Each contains the one below it; a suite names the smallest tier that runs it.
tier.clash: Not a storage tier: DittoFS's [[remote-tier|remote tier]] is where [[offload|offloaded]] content lives. A test tier says when tests run, not where data is stored.

blocking.name: blocking
blocking.short: Whether a cell's failure can fail the gate. A non-blocking cell is reported but never holds a merge.
blocking.long: A [[suite]] or option with `blocking: false` runs and is reported, its new failures annotated, but never fails the [[gate]], which doesn't wait for it. It may differ per [[tier]]: the Windows unit run is non-blocking on PRs only.

gate.name: gate
gate.short: The one CI job that decides merges: it fails unless every blocking cell exited 0.
gate.long: The `gate` job of `tests.yml`: it needs every job that runs a [[blocking]] [[cell]], always runs, joins their reports, and fails unless `plan` passed and each of them passed or was skipped. develop requires it.
gate.clash: Not the adapters' share gate (who may enter a share), nor the throughput and allocation gates: Go tests that fail on a measured threshold, run nightly, and never fail a pull request.

result-format.name: format
result-format.short: How `dt` reads a tool's results: `exit`, `go-json`, `junit`, `tap`, `subunit`, `trx` or `nfstest`.
result-format.long: A standard way a tool reports per-test results, read by one reader in `dt`; there are seven. For every format but `exit`, the results the tool writes decide, not its exit status.

ctrf.name: CTRF
ctrf.short: Common Test Report Format: the JSON every run writes as `summary.json`, with JUnit generated from it.
ctrf.long: Common Test Report Format, a JSON schema with retries, flaky passes and the tool's own status as fields. `dt` writes it at one pinned version, 0.1.0, with its [[grade|grades]] in `extra`, and generates JUnit XML from it.

grade.name: grade
grade.short: What `dt` decides about one test result, for example new, known, quarantined, unexpected pass or expected skip.
grade.long: The verdict on one result, kept in `extra.grade`: `new`, `known`, `quarantined`, `unexpected_pass`, `expected_skip`, `unexpected_skip`, `ungraded`, `incomplete`, or none for a pass. `new` and an unexpected pass exit 1; an unexpected skip and `incomplete` exit 2.

known-failure.name: known failure
known-failure.short: A test listed in its suite's `known.yaml` as failing, with a reason. It doesn't turn the run red.
known-failure.long: An entry in a suite's `known.yaml`: the test, why it fails, a category, and `fix: planned` (with its issue) or `wontfix`. `where` limits it to some matrix values, tiers, options or OS. A failure it matches is graded `known`.

expected-skip.name: expected skip
expected-skip.short: A test listed as allowed to skip, with its reason. Any other skip is lost coverage.
expected-skip.long: A `known.yaml` entry with `status: skip`. In a suite with a known file, every test that skips or doesn't execute must be one, or the [[cell]] is [[not-run|not run]]. The Go suites opt in package by package, e2e first.

unexpected-pass.name: unexpected pass
unexpected-pass.short: A listed failure or skip that passed: the cell fails, because the list no longer says what the server does.
unexpected-pass.long: A [[known-failure|known failure]] or [[expected-skip|expected skip]] whose test passed in every result it matched in the cell. It exits 1, so a fix removes its own entry. An entry marked `intermittent: true` reports the pass instead.

not-run.name: not run
not-run.short: Exit status 2, meaning something did not run: for example a need was unmet under `--ci`, the fixture failed, or, in a suite with a known-failure list, a test skipped without being listed. It never counts as a pass.
not-run.long: The result of a [[cell]] that didn't test what it claims: an unmet need under `--ci`, a [[fixture]] that failed its check or timed out, nothing ran, tests a timeout left unstarted, an incomplete result, or, in a suite with a known-failure list, an unlisted skip. Exit 2, never a pass.

quarantine.name: quarantine
quarantine.short: A list of flaky tests that still run but never fail a run or alert, each with an issue and an expiry.
quarantine.long: `test/harness/quarantine.yaml`: entries of suite, test, issue and expiry, at most 90 days ahead. The test still runs and is recorded; a failure is graded `quarantined`. A crash or a hang stays `new`. An expired entry excuses nothing.

flaky.name: flaky
flaky.short: A test that failed, then passed on retry. `dt history` counts it; it raises no alert.
flaky.long: A test that failed and then passed on [[retry]]: graded passed, with `flaky: true`. On develop it opens no [[develop-red]]; `dt history` counts it, and flaky twice in a week makes it a [[quarantine]] candidate.

retry.name: retry
retry.short: `--retry 1` runs only the new failures again, after merges and on scheduled runs, and never on pull requests.
retry.long: Running a [[cell]]'s new failures again, on its own [[fixture]]: `--retry 1` after merges and on the schedule, never on a pull request or a dispatch, so a PR can't merge a [[flaky]] test it introduced. A fixture's setup is never retried.

develop-red.name: develop-red issue
develop-red.short: A single GitHub issue, titled `develop is red`, that is rewritten in place with the tests currently failing on develop.
develop-red.long: The develop-status issue, labelled `develop-red`: opened or updated when a merge-tier or nightly run on develop still exits 1 after its [[retry]]. It closes once nothing in the set fails.

baseline.name: baseline
baseline.short: A snapshot of DittoFS's own smbtorture results, kept in a file. A developer refreshes it through a pull request; no nightly job writes it.
baseline.long: `baseline-results.md`, a snapshot of DittoFS's own smbtorture results on `badger-s3`, written with `dt known baseline` and landed through a pull request. It replaces a nightly job that pushed it and failed every night.
baseline.clash: Three things share the word: smbtorture's baseline file; the same NFS tests run against the Linux kernel's own NFS server (knfsd), for comparison; and a benchmark's stored baseline, which reports a change but never fails a run. None is a known-failure list.

control-plane.name: control plane
control-plane.short: The records that hold every setting, such as shares, users, stores and adapters. They are the one source of configuration.
control-plane.long: The records in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] that hold every setting; the one source of configuration (RFC 0, RFC 13 §2.1). Operators change them through the [[management-api|management API]], and each [[node]] reads them and makes its components match (RFC 23).
control-plane.clash: In today's code, `pkg/controlplane` is the control plane: the [[runtime]], the REST API and a database of its own (SQLite or PostgreSQL), separate from the metadata store.

management-api.name: management API
management-api.short: The one entry point for every change an operator makes. It authenticates the operator, checks the change and writes it as records.
management-api.long: The one door for every change to what an installation serves (RFC 23): it authenticates the operator, checks the change and writes it as records in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]]; it never reaches into a running component. [[dfsctl]], the Kubernetes operator and scripts are its clients. Today it is the REST API that `dfs` serves, under `/api/v1`.

runtime.name: Runtime
runtime.short: Today's composition layer inside `dfs`: the single entrypoint the adapters and the REST API both go through.
runtime.long: Today's single entrypoint for all operations (architecture.md): a thin composition of six sub-services that owns each share's block store. The RFCs replace it: the [[node]] builds the components, and adapters call the [[filesystem-service|filesystem service]] (RFC 23 Appendix B).

dfsctl.name: dfsctl
dfsctl.short: The command-line client that manages a running DittoFS server through its REST API.
dfsctl.long: The command-line client of the [[management-api|management API]]: users, groups, shares, stores and adapters on a running `dfs`. It only calls the API and never opens a store or a journal (RFC 23 §7). Its credentials live in `~/.config/dfsctl/config.json`.

epoch.name: epoch (shard epoch)
epoch.short: A number in a [[shard]]'s record that rises whenever a change must stop an older [[primary]] from acting, such as a new primary taking over. A call or commit carrying an older epoch is refused. It is not the [[node-epoch|node epoch]], which counts a node's starts.
epoch.long: A number in the shard record, raised by every change to it that must fence a sender: a takeover, a handover, a replica joining or removed, the start of a move of files. (cluster) A message carrying an older one is refused, and a commit is refused unless the file's [[fence-records|fence records]] hold exactly its (shard, epoch). Not the [[node-epoch|node epoch]] nor the [[shard-incarnation]].

node-epoch.name: node epoch
node-epoch.short: A number raised for one [[node]] each time it starts and, in a cluster, each time it takes a new [[node-lease|node lease]]. It is one of the inputs of the [[write-verifier|write verifier]].
node-epoch.long: Raised for one node at every start and, in a cluster, every new lease. A node whose lease lapsed takes a new one at a higher node epoch and is primary of nothing until it takes a shard over. The [[write-verifier]] takes it as an input, beside the journal's [[loss-generation|loss generation]]; it does not take the shard [[epoch]].

node-lease.name: node lease
node-lease.short: (cluster) The lease each [[node]] renews in the metadata store to keep serving. A node whose node lease has lapsed serves nothing.
node-lease.long: (cluster) The one lease each node renews in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]]. A node whose lease lapsed serves nothing; a [[handover|takeover]] marks its node record lapsed, and every commit on its shards checks that mark. Not a [[client-lease|client lease]], nor an SMB [[lease]].

handover.name: handover
handover.short: (cluster) A planned change of a [[shard]]'s [[primary]]. There is no wait for a lease to lapse and no grace period, because the old primary passes the shard's open state to the new one.
handover.long: (cluster) A planned change of primary, with no lease wait and no grace: the old primary ships the shard's open-state table, with its [[dedup-table|dedup]] entries, to the new one. If the old primary is lost before the new one holds the table, grace follows as after a [[takeover]]. It raises the shard's [[epoch]].

namespace-move.name: move (namespace)
namespace-move.short: Handing a group of shares, with their metadata, to another DittoFS installation (a separate set of servers with its own metadata store) that uses the same bucket, so the stored blocks stay where they are. Each share is frozen while its last changes are copied over, so none is lost. It is not a move between the nodes of one cluster.
namespace-move.long: Handing a namespace, with its shares' metadata, from one installation to another on the same bucket; the [[block|blocks]] stay where they are. While the last changes are carried over, the share is frozen, for at most `migration.freeze_timeout`, and calls on it are answered [[retry-later]]. Not a move of files between shards.

clone.name: clone
clone.short: A copy that shares content instead of copying it. A clone of a share is a new writable share made from a [[snapshot]]; a clone of part of a file reuses its uploaded [[chunk|chunks]] and copies only the bytes not yet uploaded.
clone.long: (share) A new writable [[share]] made from a complete snapshot, in the snapshot's namespace. (file) A copy of an [[extent]] of a file that adopts its carved [[ref|refs]] and copies only the bytes still [[dirty]] in the journal; a server-side copy works the same way. A [[block]] leaves the bucket only when no file, snapshot or clone uses it.

deduplication.name: deduplication
deduplication.short: Storing identical content once when several files carry it. The first release does not deduplicate across files: offload uploads every chunk it cuts.
deduplication.long: Storing content that several files carry only once. The first release does not deduplicate across files: offload never asks whether a [[chunk]] is already stored. Chunks stay named by a keyed hash of their content, and refcounts stay, because [[clone|clones]] and snapshots share chunks.
deduplication.clash: Not the [[dedup-table|dedup table]] of a forwarded call, which answers a retried request with its first result.

dedup-table.name: dedup table
dedup-table.short: (cluster) A table at the [[primary]] that keeps the result of each recent change by its request ID, so a call resent after a lost reply is answered with its first result instead of running twice.
dedup-table.long: (cluster) Kept by `vfs.Serve` at the primary: recent mutations keyed by request ID alone, each held for at least the retry window, never under 600 s. A [[handover]] ships only the entries of open-state calls, with the table they apply to.
dedup-table.clash: Not [[deduplication]] of content, which stores identical chunks once.

sync-mark.name: sync mark
sync-mark.short: What a journal [[sync]] returns for each append stream: how far its records are proven to be on the device. After a crash the journal cannot tell a synced record the device later lost from one the crash cut short, which it treats as never written. A mark recorded in the metadata store settles it, so a lost overwrite of committed content is counted as a loss.
sync-mark.long: Per [[append-stream|append stream]]: the stream, the [[segment]], its synced-through offset, and the end and sequence number of the newest record the `Sync` named. The journal returns the marks and the caller owns them, recording them in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] with the [[group-commit|group commit]]. A [[stability-point|stability point]] over committed content waits until a recorded mark covers what its `Sync` returned.

adapter-bytes.name: Adapter bytes
adapter-bytes.short: Opaque bytes, at most 4 KiB, that an [[adapter]] stores in an open-state record through the service, for protocol detail that must survive a lost connection or a restart. The open-state table stores and returns them, and never reads them.
adapter-bytes.long: The `Adapter` field of a client record and of some other open-state records: a one-slot replay of a setup call, a callback address, an NLM host's notice address. Written with the change it belongs to, through the [[filesystem-service|service]], never by the adapter itself; at most 4 KiB, starting with the adapter's own version byte. In a cluster they travel opaque in the forwarded call.

floor-bucket.name: floor bucket
floor-bucket.short: One of 4,096 version numbers the journal keeps, picked by a hash of the file ID. A [[fill]] for a file the journal holds nothing of is checked against that file's bucket, since the file has no version of its own there.
floor-bucket.long: The per-file [[change-version]] is bounded by a fixed table of 4,096 floor buckets, indexed by a hash of the `FileID`. Dropping a file's index entry raises its bucket to the entry's version. At open every bucket starts at the higher of the highest version on disk and the floor the engine passes, and attaching a share raises every bucket to that floor. A file with no entry is compared against its bucket, so a stale fill is refused even once the entry is gone.

version-limit.name: version limit
version-limit.short: The ceiling below which the journal may hand out [[content-version|versions]]. A version reaches clients, as a file's change attribute, before its record is synced, so the engine writes the ceiling durably ahead of need; after a crash the counter restarts above it and never hands a version out twice.
version-limit.long: The smallest durable per-share limit the caller wrote for the shares a journal serves (`SetVersionLimit`). A version is seen before its record syncs, so a counter rebuilt after a crash could issue it again; the limit prevents that. The engine raises it ahead by time. A change that would reach it is refused with `ErrNoSpace` naming the version limit.

admission-lock.name: admission lock
admission-lock.short: The service's per-file lock, taken first by every call that touches a file. The call holds it across a check, such as the open-state check, and the change or I/O that check allows.
admission-lock.long: The outer level of the [[open-state-step|open-state step]], keyed by file ID whether or not the file has open state. The service holds it across a compound operation: a check and the I/O or change it admits. It comes first in the [[lock-order|lock order]]. Not share [[admission]].

fold-admission.name: fold admission
fold-admission.short: The gate at a directory's [[primary]] that lets creates, removes and renames in that directory through. When the directory's pending count and time updates are due to be merged into its record (a [[delta-fold|fold]]), new changes wait until the fold commits.
fold-admission.long: A fold rewrites the directory's record, which every create, link and rename into it guards, so the primary orders them in memory: once a fold is due, it stops admitting changes to the directory, waits for those in flight, folds, then admits the queue. A change needing several directories takes them in file-ID order within its deadline, or answers [[retry-later]]. Not share [[admission]].

accept-lock.name: accept lock
accept-lock.short: A per-file lock at the file's [[primary]]. Every write, truncate or attribute change holds it while it draws its version and is applied, so the attributes captured before and after it ([[wcc|WCC]]) are exact.
accept-lock.long: Taken by every write, truncate, attribute change and setuid clearing before it draws its `Version`: around `WriteAt` for a write, the engine's `Draw` for any other change. Never held across a [[sync]] or a [[group-commit|group commit]], so a stable overwrite does not hold back the file's other changes. Last in the [[lock-order|lock order]]; the journal and the engine take no such lock.

not-yours.name: NotYours (ErrNotYours)
not-yours.short: The refusal a call gets when it uses an open, a lock or a [[caching-grant]] that belongs to another user or another client. An open can be used only by the user who opened it.
not-yours.long: Every call that uses an [[open]] (I/O through its reference, a lock under it, a downgrade, a close) is refused `ErrNotYours` unless the caller's principal is the open's. A grant that covers no open may be used only by its own client. A call without a [[session]] that presents state created on a session is refused too, whatever its principal.

handle-caching.name: handle caching
handle-caching.short: The part of an SMB [[caching-grant]] (a batch [[oplock]], or a [[lease]] with H) that lets a client keep a file open after its application has closed it, so it can reopen the file without asking the server.
handle-caching.long: A client holding it keeps an open its application already closed, with that open's [[deny-mode|deny mode]]. So before the server refuses any request for a deny-mode conflict, it breaks handle caching on the opens that cause it and answers [[retry-later]]. A holder that kept the file open only in its cache closes it, and only a conflict that remains is refused.

quota.name: quota
quota.short: A limit on the bytes and files that a share, a project (a directory tree), a user or a group may use. A write past the hard limit is refused; past the soft limit it is refused only once a grace time has run out; an advisory threshold refuses nothing.
quota.long: Each quota has a hard limit, refused beyond; a soft limit, allowed beyond for its grace time and then refused as hard; and an advisory threshold, never refused, whose crossing only emits a quota event. Usage is counted in logical bytes per file, holes excluded, even where a [[clone]] shares the content. Only the [[filesystem-service|service]] enforces it, through a [[quota-reservation]].

named-stream.name: named stream
named-stream.short: A second, named content of a file, such as SMB's `report.docx:summary`. It has its own file ID, but no name entry, owner or permissions of its own: it follows its file.
named-stream.long: A `File` of type `Stream`, its bytes in the journal like any file's. It has no entry and is reached only by listing its file's streams; every check on it is a check on its base file, and the file ID reported for it is its base file's. Its base file's [[file-release|release]] leaves it [[pending-release|pending]], and it is then released as a file of its own.

dtc.name: dtc
dtc.short: A Linux container with the pinned test tools, in which `dt` can run. A run moves into it when a suite needs something the host lacks, such as a Linux-only suite on macOS.
dtc.long: `test/harness/bin/dtc`: a privileged container with a pinned Linux toolchain, which runs the same `dt` command with `--in host`. With `--in auto`, the default, `dt` moves a whole run there when Docker is present and a [[cell]] needs what the host lacks and the container gives. A need neither can meet is reported as not run, never as passed.

system-scenario.name: system scenario
system-scenario.short: One of 42 shell scripts in `test/scenarios/`. Each starts a real server in a container, drives real SMB and NFS clients against it, and often injects a fault such as an S3 outage or a crash.
system-scenario.long: Run as the `system` [[suite]] through `test/scenarios/setup.sh`, on the [[dedicated-host|dedicated host]] only. Each is named `<number>-<what>-<size>.sh`: the first digit is its group, from 0x smoke tests to 7x outages and crashes, and the 9x scenarios are long runs, such as one that grows a 30 GB file.

floating-address.name: floating address
floating-address.short: (cluster) A client-facing IP address that belongs to the cluster rather than to one node. When the node serving it is lost, a surviving node takes the address over, so clients reconnect to the same address.
floating-address.long: (cluster) A client-facing address the cluster owns and a surviving node takes over. SMB clients of a [[continuously-available|continuously available]] share learn of a move through [[witness|Witness]]; NFS clients on hard mounts simply retry against whichever node now answers the address.

pending-release.name: pending release
pending-release.short: A record saying that a file has lost its last name and its content is still to be released. It keeps nothing alive, and after a restart recovery finishes each release it finds.
pending-release.long: Records that a file lost its last name and its content is still to be released. It keeps nothing alive. The [[file-release|release]] then runs at the file's [[primary]] through the engine's `Delete`, and after a restart recovery runs each pending release it finds, so a crash in between leaks nothing. A [[named-stream|named stream]] is left pending by its base file's release.

takeover.name: takeover (failover)
takeover.short: (cluster) An unplanned change of a [[shard]]'s [[primary]], often called a failover. The primary's [[node-lease|node lease]] has lapsed, so another node that holds a copy of the shard's writes becomes primary, and a grace period follows.
takeover.long: (cluster) A replica, a node other than the primary whose journal holds a copy of every write to the shard, becoming [[primary]] after the primary's [[node-lease|node lease]] lapsed. The old primary's open state is lost, so a [[grace-period]] follows. It raises the shard's [[epoch]], so calls still aimed at the old primary are refused. A planned change is a [[handover]].

in-memory-service.name: in-memory service
in-memory-service.short: The real filesystem service running over memory stores (`memory.New`), held to the same conformance suite as the production one. Handler tests run against it and check the state it holds afterwards.
in-memory-service.long: `memory.New`: the real `*vfs.Filesystem` over memory stores, passing the service's conformance suite. A handler test checks the encoded reply and the state the service holds afterwards: an SMB `CREATE` whose deny mode is dropped still opens the file, but a second, conflicting open that succeeds shows the field is missing. Error answers come from a fault wrapper around it that fails a named method on cue.
